s001.text: UPSC, twenty seventeen. General Studies Paper Two, fifteen marks, two hundred and fifty words. Examine the scope of Fundamental Rights in the light of the latest privacy judgment. Here is the twist. The judgment did not amend anything. It found a right already there.

s002.text: Read what it asks. Examine means weigh, and give a balanced view. There are four jobs. Say what the judgment decided. Show how it widens the scope. Say who is bound, and the limits. Then weigh it.

s003.text: Start with the decision. In August twenty seventeen, nine judges signed one order. Privacy is protected under Article twenty-one. Two older cases, Sharma and Kharak Singh, were overruled on that point.

s004.text: But how can a court add a right? It says it did not add one. Fundamental rights are recognised, not granted. Life and liberty are inalienable. The Court only recognised what was there.

s005.text: That changes the shape of Part III. In nineteen fifty, Gopalan treated rights as separate silos. Later cases made them overlap. Puttaswamy confirmed it, and overruled ADM Jabalpur.

s006.text: And the content grows. Privacy covers dignity, family life, procreation and sexual orientation. It reaches informational privacy and self-identity. It binds the State and private actors.

s007.text: But it is not unlimited. A law that invades privacy must have legality, a legitimate aim, and proportionality. In twenty eighteen the Aadhaar case applied a four-part version of that test.

s008.text: Now we write. Two hundred and fifty words, about eleven minutes. Open with the date, the nine judges and the two cases overruled. That frames the whole answer.

s009.text: Section one is the widening. Five points: recognised, overlap, evolving, new content, and the Koushal turn. The timeline draws beside it.

s010.text: Section two is who is bound, and the limits. Then section three weighs it. Scope grows by recognition, but case by case, and never without the three tests.

s011.text: Now the easy answer beside it. It says the Court amended Article twenty-one. It did not. It says privacy is absolute. It is not. It says only the State is bound. Kaul J. said otherwise. And it repeats the silos idea that the Court replaced.

s012.text: Here is the payoff. One answer serves its cousins. Twenty twenty-four asked about privacy and the DNA test. Twenty twenty-six asked about privacy and self-identity. Learn the judgment once.
